newsitem.title: UK: Wall St. jitters hit commodities, await funds' move.
newsitem.headline: Wall St. jitters hit commodities, await funds' move.

text.p: Commodity markets are holding their breath, waiting to see whether hot investment fund money will settle in commodities as soggy stock and bond markets spark a search for stronger returns.
In the short-term, metals and other commodities probably have further to fall as overheated markets correct lower, accentuated by the jitters on Wall Street and firmer interest rates, analysts said.
Nickel and coffee are down around 15 percent from their recent highs largely on fund profit-taking. Grains are bucking the trend as freezing weather in the U.S. growing areas boosts prices.

The outlook for the rest of 1997 and next year is less clear and fund managers are believed to be moving into cash, awaiting the implications of last month's rise in U.S. rates, the first in three years.
So far, they have apparently resisted piling into commodities as a traditional hedge against inflation.
Some analysts are bullish on industrial metals in the longer term, arguing that higher interest rates only occur when economies are steaming ahead and demand for metals is high.
"The very reason that interest rates are being increased is due to the health of the economy," said analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group.
"Growth in housing starts, car sales and many of the key demand indicators of metal consumption are all having to be reined back by higher interest rates," he added.
Funds will likely wait for further price falls before re-entering the market, broker GNI said in a report.

"All the current signals suggest a stronger global economy which should make them (base metals) worth buying on dips...but this could take another six weeks to two months, by which time we should be able to have a better view of the impact of the dollar," GNI added.

Since 1987, higher interest rates have correlated with rallies in the industrial metals complex, reversing an earlier trend from 1970 to 1987 when monetary tightening led to soft metals prices, analysts said.
Bullish analysts focus on the most recent trend, but others are more wary, especially now that industrial economies seemed to have entered a new low-inflation environment.
"The linkages are becoming a bit difficult to discern," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis. "Fund managers tend to be very selective, they're more sophisticated now."
They may continue to zero in on aluminium, nickel and zinc, which have the most bullish fundamentals, he said.

Gold has been hurt by the recent rise in interest rates since it raises the opportunity cost of holding bullion, but silver, platinum and palladium have mainly industrial uses and the longer term outlook is stronger if economies keep growing.
In agricultural commodities, coffee and cocoa have come off recent peaks, with funds said to be out of the market after heavy bouts of profit-taking.
Coffee rocketed by more than 50 percent early this year as tight supplies set off panic buying and fund activity.
The main focus now in the coffee market is the upcoming winter in Brazil, the world's largest coffee producer. A crop-damaging freeze would lure the funds back, analysts said.
In cocoa, funds are said to be slightly long, even after creaming off some gains, and may get restive if prices continue to stagnate, leading to another sell-off.
Grains prices, though, have been jolted by a blast of unseasonable freezing weather in the U.S. breadbasket, sending wheat prices to six-month peaks above $4.00 a bushel.
